claim: Beewolf eggs emit a conspicuous pungent smell within 24 hr after oviposition that disappears by the time the larvae hatch.
source: Thorough examination of beewolf nests in observation cages (Strohm and Linsenmair, 1994) revealed that within 24 hr after oviposition, a conspicuous pungent smell occurred that was clearly emanating from the eggs and disappeared by the time the larvae hatched.
evidence: Direct observation documented in the manuscript text

claim: Honeybees carrying a beewolf egg show significantly delayed fungus growth compared to bees without egg from oviposition to cocoon spinning (day 0-11).
source: When paralyzed honeybees from completed beewolf brood cells were incubated individually, bees carrying an egg showed significantly delayed fungus growth compared to bees without egg over the period from oviposition to cocoon spinning (Kaplan Meier survival analysis, Breslow test, day 0–11: Chi square = 12, df = 1, p=0.001; Figure 2A).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Honeybees carrying a beewolf egg show significantly delayed fungus growth compared to bees without egg from oviposition to larval hatching (day 0-3).
source: This difference was also significant for the period from oviposition to the hatching of the larvae (day 0–3: Chi square = 9.5, df = 1, p=0.002), suggesting that this effect is not due to possible antifungal mechanisms of the larvae but that it is mediated by the egg.
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Bees kept in artificial brood cells with bees carrying an egg (without physical contact) show significantly delayed fungal growth compared to control bees kept alone.
source: Two experiments supported this assumption. First, provisioned bees without wasp eggs that were kept in artificial brood cells together with bees carrying an egg (but without physical contact) showed significantly delayed fungal growth compared to control bees that were kept alone (Breslow test, day 0–11: Chi square = 7.6 df=1, p=0.006; day 0–3: Chi square = 9.1, df = 1, p=0.003; Figure 2B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Aspergillus flavus growth is entirely inhibited when exposed to volatiles from beewolf eggs for three days.
source: Second, when one of the most abundant mold species from infested beewolf brood cells, the fast growing Aspergillus flavus (Engl et al., 2016), was exposed to the volatiles presumably emanating from beewolf eggs on nutrient agar for three days, its growth was entirely inhibited, whereas it thrived in controls (for all observation times 24 hr, 48 hr, 72 hr: binomial test: N = 20, p<0.001, Figure 3).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3, with citation to prior work

claim: No fungal growth occurs in areas exposed to beewolf egg volatiles for three days after larvae are removed.
source: Notably, when the beewolf larvae were removed from the assays shortly after hatching (three days after oviposition), no fungal growth occurred in the exposed areas during another three days.
evidence: Experimental observation documented in the text

claim: Beewolf egg volatiles completely inhibit growth of five different fungal strains including A. flavus strain B, Mucor circinelloides, Penicillium roqueforti, Candida albicans and Trichophyton rubrum.
source: Analogous bioassays with five other fungal strains (A. flavus strain B, Mucor circinelloides, Penicillium roqueforti, Candida albicans and Trichophyton rubrum) revealed that in all cases fungus growth was likewise completely inhibited in the area that was exposed to volatiles from beewolf eggs, whereas the fungi thrived in the respective control areas (for each strain: N = 8, binomial test: p<0.01).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data across multiple fungal strains

claim: Beewolf eggs release a volatile compound with broad spectrum fungicidal properties.
source: We conclude that beewolf eggs release a volatile compound with broad spectrum fungicidal properties.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results showing inhibition of diverse fungal species

claim: The odor emanating from beewolf eggs is similar to that of strong oxidants like chlorine, ozone and nitrogen dioxide.
source: The odor emanating from the eggs was similar to that of strong oxidants like chlorine, ozone and nitrogen dioxide (subjective evaluation of several observers, [Mücke and Lemmen, 2010]).
evidence: Subjective observation by multiple observers with citation to reference work

claim: Beewolf egg headspace contains an oxidant as demonstrated by blue coloration in iodide/starch solution.
source: In fact, the generation of a strong blue coloration when placing a beewolf egg into the lid of a reaction tube filled with a iodide/starch solution ([Jander and Blasius, 1971], see iodometry in Materials and methods) revealed the existence of an oxidant in the headspace of beewolf eggs.
evidence: Chemical test result with citation to methodology

claim: Ozone has not been described to be synthesized by organisms.
source: Ozone has, to our knowledge, not been described to be synthesized by organisms.
evidence: Statement based on authors' knowledge of the literature

claim: Molecular chlorine occurrence in organisms seems to be restricted to phagocytosis.
source: Molecular chlorine has been reported as an intermediate in some organisms but its occurrence seems to be restricted to phagocytosis (Hazen et al., 1996).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work

claim: Insect embryos synthesize small amounts of nitric oxide as signaling effectors for developmental processes.
source: Insect embryos synthesize small amounts of nitric oxide (NO⋅) as signaling effectors for developmental processes (Andersen et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work

claim: NO⋅ spontaneously reacts with oxygen to yield NO2⋅.
source: If such odorless NO⋅ was emitted from the egg, it would spontaneously react with oxygen (Soegiarto et al., 2003; Mur et al., 2011) to yield the strong-smelling NO2⋅.
evidence: Chemical reaction described with citations to prior work

claim: NO⋅ and NO2⋅ show considerable antimycotic activity.
source: Moreover, belonging to the reactive nitrogen species (RNS), NO⋅ and NO2⋅ show considerable antimycotic activity (Fang, 1997; Lai et al., 2011) that would explain the observed fungicidal effect of beewolf eggs.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work

claim: Headspace samples of confined beewolf eggs test positive for NO⋅ and NO2⋅ using the Griess assay.
source: We tested whether beewolf eggs produce and emit NO⋅ and/or NO2⋅ by conducting a series of experiments. First, headspace samples of confined beewolf eggs were subjected to the Griess assay, the standard procedure for the specific detection of NO⋅ and NO2⋅ (Tsikas, 2007). The emerging red color of the resulting azo dye (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) clearly indicated the presence of NO⋅/NO2⋅.
evidence: Chemical assay result with citation to methodology and reference to figure

claim: DAR4M-AM solution droplets on bees carrying freshly laid eggs show clear fluorescence that increases over several hours.
source: To visualize the emission of NO⋅ from beewolf eggs, we sprayed a solution of an NO⋅ specific fluorescent probe, Diaminorhodamin-4M AM (DAR4M-AM), onto prey bees carrying freshly laid eggs. The small droplets of the DAR4M-AM solution on the bees showed a clear fluorescence around the egg that increased over several hours (Figure 4B).
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy observation shown in Figure 4B

claim: Control bees without eggs show no fluorescence when sprayed with DAR4M-AM solution.
source: No such effect was seen on control bees without eggs (Figure 4A).
evidence: Control experiment shown in Figure 4A

claim: Beewolf eggs injected with DAR4M-AM solution show strong fluorescence that peaks about one day after oviposition.
source: Moreover, beewolf eggs injected with the DAR4M-AM solution showed a strong fluorescence that peaked about one day after oviposition (N = 45, Figure 5A).
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Eggs of Ampulex compressa injected with DAR4M-AM show only weak fluorescence.
source: The same treatment yielded only weak fluorescence in the eggs of two other Hymenoptera (the Emerald cockroach wasp, Ampulex compressa, N = 9, and the Red mason bee, Osmia bicornis, N = 12; Figure 5C and D)
evidence: Comparative fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Eggs of Osmia bicornis injected with DAR4M-AM show only weak fluorescence.
source: The same treatment yielded only weak fluorescence in the eggs of two other Hymenoptera (the Emerald cockroach wasp, Ampulex compressa, N = 9, and the Red mason bee, Osmia bicornis, N = 12; Figure 5C and D)
evidence: Comparative fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and D

claim: Newly hatched beewolf larvae injected with DAR4M-AM show only weak fluorescence.
source: The same treatment yielded only weak fluorescence in the eggs of two other Hymenoptera (the Emerald cockroach wasp, Ampulex compressa, N = 9, and the Red mason bee, Osmia bicornis, N = 12; Figure 5C and D) and in newly hatched beewolf larvae (N = 4, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy data shown in supplemental figure

claim: Autofluorescence of beewolf eggs injected with buffer only is negligible.
source: Autofluorescence of beewolf eggs injected with buffer only (N = 10) was negligible (Figure 5B).
evidence: Control experiment shown in Figure 5B

claim: Beewolf eggs produce and release NO⋅.
source: These findings strongly imply that beewolf eggs produce and release NO⋅.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including Griess assay and fluorescence microscopy

claim: A beewolf egg emits on average 0.25 ± 0.09 µmol NO⋅.
source: Using iodometry, we determined that a beewolf egg (volume: 4.1 ± 0.5 mm3, N = 16) emits on average 0.25 ± 0.09 µmol NO⋅ (N = 233).
evidence: Quantitative measurement using iodometry

claim: The rate of NO⋅ production by beewolf eggs peaks 14-15 hr after oviposition at 28°C.
source: The rate of NO⋅ production was initially very low, but increased to a distinct peak 14–15 hr (at 28°C) after oviposition (Figure 6); around 90% of NO⋅ emission occurred within a two-hour period.
evidence: Time course data shown in Figure 6

claim: Around 90% of NO⋅ emission from beewolf eggs occurs within a two-hour period.
source: The rate of NO⋅ production was initially very low, but increased to a distinct peak 14–15 hr (at 28°C) after oviposition (Figure 6); around 90% of NO⋅ emission occurred within a two-hour period.
evidence: Time course data shown in Figure 6

claim: Nitrogen oxides would accumulate to average concentrations of 1690 ± 680 ppm in beewolf brood cells assuming no loss.
source: Assuming no loss due to reactions or leaking out of the confined space of brood cells (volume 3.2 ± 0.9 cm3, N = 250), the nitrogen oxides would accumulate to average concentrations of 1690 ± 680 ppm.
evidence: Calculation based on measured NO⋅ emission and brood cell volume

claim: The timing of onset of NO⋅ emission is strongly temperature dependent with a Q10 of 2.74.
source: The timing of the onset of NO⋅ emission was strongly temperature dependent (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), with higher temperatures resulting in an earlier NO⋅production (temperature coefficient Q10 = 2.74).
evidence: Temperature dependence data shown in supplemental figure with calculated Q10 value

claim: Synthetic NO⋅ at 1500ppm significantly delays fungus growth on honeybees compared to nitrogen controls.
source: There was a significant delay in the onset of fungus growth on the bees exposed to synthetic NO⋅ as compared to controls (Figure 7, Breslow test: Chi square = 13.3, df = 1, p<0.0001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7

claim: The onset of fungal growth differs significantly among treatment groups combining embalming and egg presence.
source: Bioassays with bees in artificial brood cells that were either embalmed or not and carried an egg or not revealed that the onset of fungal growth differed significantly among treatment groups (Figure 8: Kaplan Meier survival analysis, Breslow test: Chi square = 69.6, df = 3, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 8

claim: Fungus growth is first detected on unembalmed honeybees without eggs, followed by embalmed bees without eggs, then unembalmed bees with eggs, and least on embalmed bees with eggs.
source: Pairwise comparisons showed that, on average, fungus growth was first detected on honeybees that had not been embalmed and did not carry an egg, second were prey items that were embalmed but did not carry and egg, third were not embalmed honeybees carrying an egg and least susceptible were embalmed honeybees with an egg (Breslow test for all pairwise comparisons: Chi square ≥8.6, df = 1, p≤0.003).
evidence: Statistical analysis of pairwise comparisons

claim: The timing of conidia formation follows the same pattern as fungal hyphae appearance across treatment groups.
source: The timing of conidia formation followed the same pattern (Breslow test: Chi square = 67.4, df = 3, p<0.001; for all pairwise comparisons: Chi square ≥4.5, df = 1, p≤0.034; Figure 8).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 8

claim: Eukaryotes synthesize NO⋅ from L-arginine by the enzyme nitric oxide synthase (NOS).
source: Eukaryotes synthesize NO⋅ from the amino acid L-arginine by the enzyme nitric oxide synthase (NOS) (Röszer, 2012) which is highly conserved also in insects (Regulski and Tully, 1995).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work

claim: NOS is highly conserved in insects.
source: Eukaryotes synthesize NO⋅ from the amino acid L-arginine by the enzyme nitric oxide synthase (NOS) (Röszer, 2012) which is highly conserved also in insects (Regulski and Tully, 1995).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work

claim: NADPH-diaphorase assay shows strong blue staining only in embryonic tissue of beewolf eggs, indicating NOS activity.
source: The fixation insensitive nicotinamide-adenine-dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) -diaphorase assay resulted in strong blue staining only in embryonic tissue (Figure 9), thus indicating NOS activity.
evidence: Histological staining result shown in Figure 9

claim: The temporal expression pattern of NOS-mRNA shows a clear peak around 19-20 hr after oviposition at 25°C.
source: Second, by employing reverse transcription and real time quantitative PCR, we revealed that the temporal expression pattern of NOS-mRNA showed a clear peak around 19–20 hr after oviposition (Figure 10). For this experiment, the eggs were kept at 25°C, so the timing of peak NOS expression corresponds to the timing of peak NO⋅ emission at this temperature (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 10 with reference to temperature-dependent NO⋅ emission data

claim: Injection of beewolf eggs with L-NAME causes a significant decrease in NO⋅ emission.
source: Third, to directly test for the involvement of NOS we injected beewolf eggs with Nω-nitro-L-arginine methylester (L-NAME), a NOS-inhibiting analog of L-arginine (Willmot et al., 2005). This treatment caused a significant decrease in NO⋅ emission, whereas the non-inhibiting enantiomer D-NAME had no such effect (Figure 11).
evidence: Inhibition assay data shown in Figure 11 with citation to methodology

claim: The non-inhibiting enantiomer D-NAME has no effect on NO⋅ emission from beewolf eggs.
source: This treatment caused a significant decrease in NO⋅ emission, whereas the non-inhibiting enantiomer D-NAME had no such effect (Figure 11).
evidence: Control experiment data shown in Figure 11

claim: Most invertebrates appear to have only one type of NOS.
source: In contrast to vertebrates, most invertebrates appear to have only one type of NOS (Rivero, 2006; Whitten et al., 2007).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work

claim: The beewolf genome contains only one NOS gene copy comprising 9.36 kbp with 25 exons.
source: Sequencing of the NOS-gene(s) of P. triangulum (Pt-NOS) revealed only one Pt-NOS copy in the beewolf genome comprising 9.36 kbp with 25 exons (Figure 11—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Gene sequencing data with reference to supplemental figure

claim: The beewolf NOS amino acid sequence shows high similarity to the NOS of closely related bees.
source: A phylogenetic analysis of the resulting amino acid sequence revealed a high similarity to the NOS of the closely related bees (Apidae, Figure 11—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis shown in supplemental figure

claim: The NOS-mRNA of beewolf eggs lacks exon 14 comprising 144 bp, in contrast to adult beewolves and honeybees.
source: However, mRNA sequencing showed that, in contrast to adult beewolves and honeybees, the NOS-mRNA of beewolf eggs (3.72 kbp) lacks exon 14 comprising 144 bp.
evidence: mRNA sequencing data comparing eggs to adults

claim: In adult beewolf NOS-mRNA, exon 14 is located between the binding domains for calmodulin and flavin mononucleotide (FMN).
source: In the NOS-mRNA of adult beewolves this exon is located between the binding domains for calmodulin and flavin mononucleotide (FMN) (Figure 11—figure supplement 1).
evidence: mRNA sequencing and structural analysis shown in supplemental figure

claim: Beewolves have evolved at least three different antimicrobial defenses that provide protection during development.
source: In fact, beewolf progeny and their provisions are under severe threat from fast growing mold fungi (Strohm and Linsenmair, 2001). The development of beewolf progeny from oviposition to cocoon spinning lasts about 11 days and is, thus, rather fast. So even a few days delay in fungus growth provides a considerable benefit for the larvae. Beewolves have evolved at least three very different antimicrobial defenses that provide an effective, coordinated, and long-term protection against a broad spectrum of microbes during the whole development.
evidence: Summary statement with citation to prior work

claim: During winter diapause, beewolf progeny are protected by antibiotics on their cocoons produced by symbiotic Streptomyces bacteria.
source: First, throughout the long period of winter diapause prior to emergence progeny are protected by antibiotics on their cocoons that are produced by symbiotic Streptomyces bacteria (Kaltenpoth et al., 2005; Kroiss et al., 2010; Kaltenpoth et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work

claim: During early egg and larval stages, molding of provisions is retarded by embalming of honeybees with lipids by the mother wasp.
source: Second, during the early egg and larval stages, molding of the provisions is retarded by an embalming of the honeybees with lipids by the mother wasp (Strohm and Linsenmair, 2001).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work

claim: The emission of gaseous nitrogen oxide radicals by beewolf eggs kills detrimental fungi in their immediate environment.
source: Third, as shown here, the emission of gaseous nitrogen oxide radicals by the beewolf egg results not only in delay of molding but in killing of detrimental fungi in their immediate environment thus, at least partly, eliminating this major threat.
evidence: Summary of findings from current study

claim: The estimated maximum concentration of nitrogen oxides in beewolf brood cells is around 1500 ppm or 60 µmol/l.
source: However, even assuming some loss during the two hour period of peak NO⋅ production the estimated maximum concentration of nitrogen oxides (NO⋅ and NO2⋅) in beewolf brood cells (probably around 1500 ppm or 60 µmol/l) considerably exceeds the concentrations observed in animal tissues (mostly lower than 0.1 µmol/l [Wink et al., 2011], 0.85–1.3µmol/l in muscle tissue [Vaughn et al., 1998]).
evidence: Calculation with citations to comparative values from prior work

claim: The maximum NO⋅/NO2⋅ concentration in beewolf brood cells might be higher than concentrations used in medical applications against multiple drug resistant bacteria (200 ppm NO⋅).
source: The maximum concentration in beewolf brood cells might be even higher than what is used in medical applications against multiple drug resistant bacteria (200 ppm NO⋅[Ghaffari et al., 2006]) or in antifungal treatment of fruit (50–500 ppm NO⋅[Lazar et al., 2008]) and is far beyond permissible exposure limits for humans (e.g. for the USA: 25 ppm for NO⋅, 5 ppm for NO2⋅[Administration USOSaH, 2014]).
evidence: Comparison with citations to medical applications and safety standards

claim: The antifungal effect of brood cell fumigation by beewolf eggs is predominantly or exclusively due to NO⋅ and its oxidation product NO2⋅.
source: Although we cannot exclude that small amounts of other active volatiles are released by beewolf eggs, we thus conclude that the antifungal effect of brood cell fumigation by beewolf eggs is predominantly or exclusively due to NO⋅ and its oxidation product NO2⋅.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of synthetic NO⋅ effects with egg-produced gas effects

claim: The combination of prey embalming and brood cell fumigation with NO⋅/NO2⋅ affects fungal growth beyond either antimicrobial measure alone.
source: Notably, the combination of prey embalming with unsaturated hydrocarbons that reduces condensation of water on the bees (Herzner and Strohm, 2007) and brood cell fumigation with NO⋅/NO2⋅ seems to affect fungal growth beyond either of these antimicrobial measures alone.
evidence: Inference from experimental data with citation to prior work on embalming mechanism

claim: NO⋅ and NO2⋅ dissolve in water to yield nitric acid and nitrous acid, with nitrous acid being a potent antibacterial agent.
source: One possible explanation is based on the fact that NO⋅ and NO2⋅ dissolve in water (confirmed by the spraying of a bee with a fluorescent dye, Figure 4) to yield nitric acid and nitrous acid, with the latter being a potent antibacterial agent (Gao et al., 2015).
evidence: Chemical knowledge with citation and reference to experimental confirmation

claim: NO⋅ is an ancient biological effector of immense importance for all kinds of organisms ranging from prokaryotes to higher plants and animals.
source: NO⋅ is an ancient biological effector of immense importance for all kinds of organisms ranging from prokaryotes to higher plants and animals (Röszer, 2012; Moroz and Kohn, 2007).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work

claim: In vertebrates, NO⋅ is synthesized from L-arginine by three different isoforms of NOS encoded by different genes.
source: In vertebrates, NO⋅ is synthesized from L-arginine by three different isoforms of NOS that are encoded by different genes (Röszer, 2012; Moroz and Kohn, 2007).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work

claim: Low levels of NO (<1µmol/l) are produced by constitutive NOS isoforms and have signaling functions.
source: Low levels of NO (<1µmol/l) are produced by constitutive NOS (cNOS) isoforms (endothelial eNOS, neuronal nNOS) and have signaling functions, for example in neuronal development and in the regulation of vascular tone in vertebrates.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of NOS function

claim: Higher NO⋅ concentrations (1-10 µmol/l) are generated by inducible NOS (iNOS) and are highly cytotoxic.
source: Higher NO⋅ concentrations (1–10 µmol/l, [Thomas et al., 2003]) are generated by an inducible NOS (iNOS). At such levels NO⋅ is highly cytotoxic (Thomas et al., 2003), making it a powerful antimicrobial (Fang, 1997; Lai et al., 2011), for example in macrophages (Röszer, 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work

claim: In living tissues, NO⋅ is usually removed within seconds by reacting with the heme group of molecules such as oxyhemoglobin.
source: In living tissues, NO⋅ is usually removed within seconds by reacting with the heme group of molecules such as oxyhemoglobin (Beckman and Koppenol, 1996; Wink et al., 2011) (very low concentrations may still persist for hours [Moroz and Kohn, 2007]).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work

claim: In air, the autooxidation of NO⋅ to NO2⋅ is comparatively slow so that NO⋅ may persist for several seconds to minutes or even hours.
source: In air, the autooxidation to NO2⋅ is comparatively slow so that NO⋅ may persist (depending on its concentration) for several seconds to minutes (Mur et al., 2011; Wink et al., 2011) or even hours (Soegiarto et al., 2003).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work

claim: NO⋅ emitted by beewolf eggs might directly affect fungi by damaging DNA or inhibiting cytochrome enzymes.
source: Thus, the NO⋅ emitted by beewolf eggs might directly affect fungi, for exapmle by damaging DNA (Lai et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2010) or by reacting with the heme group of enzymes like cytochrome P450 and cytochrome c oxidase, thus inhibiting these crucial components of the mitochondrial respiratory chain (Thomas et al., 2003; Feelisch, 2008; Canessa and Larrondo, 2013).
evidence: Speculation based on citations to known mechanisms of NO⋅ action

claim: Most of the antimicrobial activity of NO⋅ is attributed to indirect effects via reactive nitrogen species, particularly NO2⋅, N2O3, and peroxynitrite.
source: Yet, most of the antimicrobial activity of NO⋅ is attributed to indirect effects via reactive nitrogen species (RNS), in particular nitrogen oxides (NO2⋅, N2O3) and peroxynitrite (ONOO-, upon reaction with superoxide) (Thomas et al., 2003).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work

claim: NO2⋅ is severely cytotoxic, for example by nitration of tyrosine residues and oxidation of proteins and lipids.
source: NO2⋅, has been reported to be severely cytotoxic, for example by nitration of tyrosine residues and oxidation of proteins and lipids (Fang, 1997; Bogdan, 2001).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work

claim: A beewolf egg of approximately 5 mg emits 0.25 µmol NO⋅ within about 2.5 hr, or 20,000 µmol/kg*h.
source: A beewolf egg of approximately 5 mg emits 0.25 µmol NO⋅ within a period of about 2.5 hr, or 20.000 µmol/kg*h, a value that is about four orders of magnitude higher than reported baseline levels of NO⋅ synthesis in humans (0.15 - ~ 4.5 µmol/kg*h [Castillo et al., 1996], rats (0.6–9 µmol/kg*h [Wu et al., 1999]) and plants (Arabidopsis thaliana, 0.36–3 µmol/kg*h [Zeidler et al., 2004]), and even considerably higher than in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-activated macrophages (~800 µmol/kg*h, estimated from Wu et al., 1999).
evidence: Calculation based on measured data with citations to comparative values

claim: NADPH diaphorase assay indicates NOS activity in embryonic tissue but not in other parts of beewolf eggs.
source: First, a specific histochemical assay indicated NOS activity in embryonic tissue but not in other parts of the egg.
evidence: Summary of histochemical assay results

claim: Quantitative PCR revealed elevated expression of the NOS gene at the time of peak NO⋅ production.
source: Second, quantitative PCR revealed elevated expression of the NOS gene at the time of peak NO⋅ production.
evidence: Summary of qPCR results

claim: Competitive inhibition of NOS by L-NAME causes a significant reduction in NO⋅ production.
source: Finally, competitive inhibition of NOS by L-NAME caused a significant reduction in NO⋅ production.
evidence: Summary of inhibition assay results

claim: A NOS located in the embryonic tissue is involved in NO⋅ production of beewolf eggs.
source: While each of the three results might have alternative explanations (e.g. L-NAME might not be a perfectly specific NOS inhibitor [Peterson et al., 1992]), taken together these findings provide strong evidence that a NOS, located in the embryonic tissue, is involved in NO⋅ production of beewolf eggs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence with acknowledgment of limitations

claim: The structure of the Pt-NOS gene is largely homologous to other insects, for example Anopheles stephensi mosquitoes.
source: Moreover, the structure of the Pt-NOS gene is largely homologous to other insects, for example Anopheles stephensi mosquitoes (Luckhart et al., 1998).
evidence: Comparison of gene structure with citation to prior work

claim: Alternative splicing resulting in different NOS-mRNAs, including deletion of exons, has been documented in A. stephensi in response to Plasmodium infection.
source: Such alternative splicing that results in different NOS-mRNAs, including the deletion of exons (but others than in beewolves), has been documented in A. stephensi in response to Plasmodium infection (Luckhart and Li, 2001).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work

claim: NOS splice variants may result in organ-specific enzymes in various organisms.
source: Moreover, NOS splice variants may result in organ-specific enzymes in other organisms (Röszer, 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work

claim: Calmodulin is believed to be responsible for NOS regulation.
source: Since calmodulin is believed to be responsible for NOS regulation (Smith et al., 2013) the deletion of an adjacent part might affect the control of NOS activity in beewolf eggs.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work

claim: The alternative splicing in beewolf eggs might enable the production of large amounts of NO⋅.
source: Thus, the alternative splicing might enable the production of such large amounts of NO⋅.
evidence: Speculation based on structural analysis

claim: The inducible NOS isoform of vertebrates (iNOS) lacks a section of about 40 amino acids (120 bp) near the FMN domain.
source: Notably, compared to the cNOS (comprising eNOS, and nNOS) the inducible NOS isoform of vertebrates (iNOS) that generates higher concentrations of NO⋅ to combat microbes lacks a section of about 40 amino acids (120 bp) near the FMN domain.
evidence: Statement based on known structural differences in vertebrate NOS isoforms

claim: The section missing in vertebrate iNOS is thought to be responsible for autoinhibition of cNOS, and its lack enhances NO⋅ production by iNOS.
source: Interestingly, this section is thought to be responsible for autoinhibition of the cNOS (Salerno et al., 1997) and its lack enhances NO⋅ production by the iNOS.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work

claim: The similarity between vertebrate iNOS and beewolf egg NOS regarding the missing section might suggest convergent modification to achieve high NO⋅ synthetic capacity.
source: The conspicuous similarity between vertebrate iNOS and the NOS in beewolf eggs with regard to the length of the missing section and its position might suggest a convergent modification to achieve a NOS with high synthetic capacity.
evidence: Speculation based on structural comparison

claim: Vertebrates have evolved another gene for iNOS, while beewolf eggs might accomplish a similar effect by alternative splicing of the mRNA.
source: Whereas vertebrates have evolved another gene, beewolf eggs might accomplish a similar effect by alternative splicing of the mRNA.
evidence: Speculation comparing evolutionary mechanisms

claim: In beewolf eggs, the activity of NOS is likely regulated by gene expression like the NOS in Plasmodium infested A. stephensi and the iNOS of vertebrates.
source: The possible loss of regulation of the NOS and the pattern of Pt-NOS expression in the eggs suggest that in beewolf eggs the activity of the enzyme is regulated by gene expression like the NOS in Plasmodium infested A. stephensi (Luckhart et al., 1998) and the iNOS of vertebrates (Wong et al., 1996; Morris Jr, 1999).
evidence: Inference from expression pattern with citations to comparable systems

claim: In beewolf eggs, expression of Pt-NOS seems to occur obligatorily at a certain stage in embryo development, not induced by immunostimulants.
source: However, in contrast to these caes, in beewolf eggs expression of the Pt-NOS seems not to be induced by immunostimulants but to occur obligatorily at a certain stage in the development of the beewolf embryo.
evidence: Inference from temporal expression pattern

claim: The NOS and its alternative splice variant likely play a significant role in brood cell fumigation by beewolf eggs.
source: While we cannot exclude that there is an additional, yet unknown, pathway of NO⋅ production in beewolf eggs, we hypothesize that the NOS and in particular its alternative splice variant plays a significant role in brood cell fumigation by beewolf eggs.
evidence: Hypothesis based on multiple lines of evidence with acknowledgment of limitations

claim: Even the combined effect of prey embalming and brood cell fumigation does not provide perfect protection, as fungus infestation still causes 5% larval mortality in the field.
source: However, even the combined effect of prey embalming and brood cell fumigation does not provide perfect protection as fungus infestation still causes larval mortality in 5% of the brood cells in the field (Strohm and Linsenmair, 2001).
evidence: Statement with citation to prior field data

claim: It seems unlikely that ubiquitous mold fungi have evolved resistance against the toxic effects of NO⋅/NO2⋅ in beewolf brood cells.
source: Another possibility, namely that strains of the ubiquitous mold fungi that are the main causes of molding in beewolf brood cells (Engl et al., 2016), have evolved resistance against the toxic effects of NO⋅/NO2⋅ seems rather unlikely.
evidence: Speculation with citation to prior work on fungal species

claim: There will be only weak selection for resistance in fungi since beewolf brood cells are a rare habitat for ubiquitous mold fungi.
source: Ultimately, there will be only weak selection for resistance at all since beewolf brood cells are certainly a rare habitat for the ubiquitous mold fungi (Engl et al., 2018).
evidence: Reasoning with citation to prior work

claim: There will be no repeated exposure of the same fungal strains to fumigation that would be required to favor the evolution of resistance.
source: Moreover, there will be no repeated exposure of the same fungal strains to fumigation that would be required to favor the evolution of resistance.
evidence: Reasoning about evolutionary dynamics

claim: The NO⋅/NO2⋅ levels emitted by beewolf eggs are very high and likely affect several basic biochemical processes, making evolution of effective resistance unlikely.
source: While there are examples for detoxification of lower concentrations of NO⋅ (mainly by scavengers like flavohemoglobins) in different fungi, including species of Aspergillus (Martins et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2009), the NO⋅/NO2⋅ levels emitted by beewolf eggs are very high and likely affect several very basic biochemical processes, thus making the evolution of an effective resistance unlikely.
evidence: Reasoning with citations to known detoxification mechanisms

claim: Brood cell fumigation might harm the symbiotic Streptomyces bacteria that beewolf females apply to the brood cell prior to egg laying.
source: While brood cell fumigation clearly retards molding of larval provisions, the antimicrobial effect of NO⋅ and NO2⋅ might harm the symbiotic Streptomyces bacteria that beewolf females apply to the brood cell prior to egg laying (Kaltenpoth et al., 2005; Kroiss et al., 2010).
evidence: Speculation with citations to prior work on symbiotic bacteria

claim: A considerable number of symbiotic bacteria have to survive brood cell fumigation since they are important for larval survival and are vertically transmitted.
source: Since the symbiotic bacteria are important for the survival of larvae in the cocoon and are vertically transmitted from beewolf mothers to their daughters (Kaltenpoth et al., 2014), a considerable number of symbionts have to survive the brood cell fumigation.
evidence: Reasoning with citation to prior work on symbiont importance

claim: The symbiotic bacteria might have evolved mechanisms to cope with high concentrations of NO⋅/NO2⋅ due to specialization and repeated exposure.
source: Conceivably, because of strong selection due to specialization and repeated exposition, the symbiotic bacteria have evolved mechanisms to cope with the high concentrations of NO⋅/NO2⋅ (Poole, 2005; Wareham et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculation with citations to mechanisms of bacterial NO⋅ resistance

claim: The bacteria being applied to the ceiling of the brood cell might reduce negative effects of nitrogen oxides since these are heavier than air.
source: Moreover, the bacteria are applied to the ceiling of the brood cell, which might reduce negative effects of the nitrogen oxides since these are heavier than air (Lide, 1995) and will accumulate in the lower part of the brood cell.
evidence: Speculation based on physical properties with citation

claim: The bacteria being embedded in copious amounts of hydrocarbon secretion might shield them from the fumigants.
source: Additionally, the bacteria are embedded in copious amounts of a secretion consisting of mostly unsaturated hydrocarbons (Kaltenpoth et al., 2009) that might shield the bacteria from the fumigants.
evidence: Speculation with citation to prior work on bacterial secretion

claim: Host- and/or symbiont-derived antioxidants in the hydrocarbon matrix could detoxify NO⋅ and NO2⋅ and protect the symbiotic Streptomyces bacteria.
source: Finally, host- and/or symbiont derived antioxidants in the hydrocarbon matrix could detoxify NO⋅ and NO2⋅ and protect the symbiotic Streptomyces bacteria.
evidence: Speculation about potential protective mechanisms

claim: It has been assumed that the primary purpose of NO⋅ was signaling at low concentrations and that antimicrobial functions at higher concentrations are derived.
source: Generally, it has been assumed that the primary purpose of NO⋅ was signaling at low concentrations and that the antimicrobial functions of higher concentrations are derived (Fang, 2004).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work

claim: Small amounts of NO⋅ originally produced for developmental processes might have accidentally been released into brood cells and slightly affected fungal germination or growth.
source: Assuming a similar scenario for beewolves, small amounts of NO⋅ that were originally produced for developmental processes (Andersen et al., 2013) might have accidentally been released into the confines of the subterranean brood cell and slightly affected the germination or growth of fungi by interfering with regulatory processes (Röszer, 2012; Wang and Higgins, 2005).
evidence: Speculation about evolutionary origin with citations to prior work

claim: Initial benefits from accidental NO⋅ release would have caused strong selection for elevated NO⋅ emission by eggs, considerably increasing progeny survival.
source: Given the severe threat posed by microbes, such initial benefits would have caused strong selection for elevated NO⋅ emission by the eggs. This would have considerably increased progeny survival and might have allowed ancestral beewolves to nest in an expanded range of habitat types, including nesting sites with high risk of microbial infestation, or to exploit highly susceptible but readily available prey species.
evidence: Speculation about evolutionary dynamics and consequences

claim: Brood cell fumigation with large doses of NO⋅ represents a key evolutionary innovation.
source: Brood cell fumigation with large doses of NO⋅ thus represents a key evolutionary innovation.
evidence: Conclusion based on evolutionary reasoning

claim: Brood cell fumigation can be viewed as an innate, externalized immune defense of beewolf eggs.
source: Since NO⋅ is used as an antimicrobial in the immune systems of many animals (Bogdan et al., 2000), its deployment as an antifungal gas can be viewed as an innate, externalized immune defense of beewolf eggs.
evidence: Interpretation with citation to prior work on NO⋅ in immune systems

claim: Externalized components of the immune system have recently been recognized as important and possibly widespread antimicrobial measures.
source: Such externalized components of the immune system have recently been recognized as important and possibly widespread antimicrobial measures (Otti et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work

claim: The clear benefit of brood cell fumigation is probably accompanied by substantial costs in terms of energy and biochemical resources.
source: The clear benefit of brood cell fumigation, however, is probably accompanied by substantial costs in terms of energy and biochemical resources (Rivero, 2006).
evidence: Inference with citation to prior work on costs

claim: L-arginine is an essential amino acid for most insects.
source: NO⋅ is synthesized from L-arginine, an amino acid that is an important constituent of many proteins and biochemical pathways (Morris Jr, 2000) and it is an essential amino acid for most insects (Barbehenn et al., 1999; Payne and Loomis, 2006) (e.g. phytophagous insects [Berenbaum, 1995], mosquitos [Uchida, 1993], aphids [Sasaki and Ishikawa, 1995; Akman Gündüz and Douglas, 2009], butterflies [Erhardt and Rusterholz, 1998; O'Brien et al., 2003], true bugs [Mesquita et al., 2015], parasitoid wasps [Thompson, 1976; Barrett and Schmidt, 1991], bees [de Groot, 1952; Weiner et al., 2010]).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work across insect taxa

claim: Beewolves have either evolved the capacity to synthesize L-arginine or female beewolves must provide each egg with sufficient L-arginine for both fumigation and embryogenesis.
source: Thus, beewolves have either evolved the capacity to synthesize L-arginine or female beewolves have to provide each egg with sufficient L-arginine for both brood cell fumigation and embryogenesis.
evidence: Inference from L-arginine requirements

claim: NO⋅ synthesis by NOS requires the cofactors FAD, FMN, BH4 and NADPH, competing with other metabolic pathways.
source: Moreover, NO⋅ synthesis by NOS requires the cofactors flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), FMN, (6R-)5,6,7,8-tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) and NADPH (Förstermann and Sessa, 2012), thus competing with other metabolic pathways in the developing beewolf embryo.
evidence: Statement with citation to prior work on NOS cofactor requirements

claim: The embryos inside beewolf eggs survive the high concentrations of toxic nitrogen oxides during synthesis, emission, and after release to the brood cell.
source: One of the most remarkable aspects of our study is that the embryos inside the egg survive the high concentrations of toxic nitrogen oxides during synthesis and emission as well as after its release to the brood cell.
evidence: Observation from experimental data

claim: Beewolf larvae that were accidentally exposed to the gas emitted by eggs died.
source: This is all the more surprising since beewolf larvae that were accidentally exposed to the gas emitted by eggs died (Strohm, unpublished observations).
evidence: Unpublished observation

claim: The synthesis and emission of high amounts of NO⋅ likely requires concomitant adaptations that protect beewolf embryos against cytotoxic effects.
source: The synthesis and emission of such high amounts of NO⋅ likely requires a number of concomitant adaptations that protect beewolf embryos against the cytotoxic effects of high concentrations of NO⋅ and NO2⋅.
evidence: Inference from survival of embryos despite high NO⋅ levels

claim: One possibility for NO⋅ tolerance is the employment of carrier molecules to transfer NO⋅ to the egg shell.
source: One possibility is the employment of carrier molecules to transfer NO⋅ to the egg shell. In blood sucking hemipterans, for example, nitrophorins carry NO⋅ to its release site to dilate blood vessels (Davies, 2000).
evidence: Speculation with citation to analogous system

claim: Understanding how beewolf eggs avoid toxic effects of NO⋅ might inspire development of novel medical applications.
source: The mechanistic basis of NO⋅ tolerance of beewolf eggs is of particular interest, since excessive production of NO⋅ due to inflammatory processes (Guzik et al., 2003) or certain diseases (e.g. Alzheimer's disease, [Lüth et al., 2002; Pacher et al., 2007; Calabrese et al., 2007; Pautz et al., 2010]) might cause severe pathological complications in humans. Thus, understanding how beewolf eggs avoid the toxic effects of NO⋅ might inspire the development of novel medical applications.
evidence: Speculation about potential applications with citations to medical relevance

claim: Sanitizing the brood cell environment by producing high amounts of NO⋅ significantly enhances the survival of immatures by reducing fungal growth on their provisions.
source: Our findings reveal a surprising adaptation in a mass-provisioning digger wasp to cope with the threat of pathogen infestation in the vulnerable egg and larval stages. Sanitizing the brood cell environment by producing high amounts of NO⋅ significantly enhances the survival of immatures by reducing fungal growth on their provisions.
evidence: Summary conclusion from experimental findings

claim: Gaseous defenses might be more widespread and underappreciated among digger wasps and bees that mass-provision and develop underground.
source: Given that mass-provisioning and development underground are widespread ecological features among digger wasps and bees and considering the difficulties of detecting volatiles in subterranean nests, such gaseous defenses might be more widespread and as yet underappreciated.
evidence: Speculation based on ecological considerations

claim: Beewolves offer unique opportunities to elucidate general questions on the evolution and regulation of NOS as well as the production of and resistance to high concentrations of NO⋅.
source: In addition to revealing new perspectives on antimicrobial strategies in nature and amplifying the biological significance of NO⋅, beewolves offer unique opportunities to elucidate general questions on the evolution and regulation of NOS as well as the production of and resistance to high concentrations of NO⋅.
evidence: Statement about research implications

claim: Without any countermeasures, beewolf provisions will be completely overgrown by mold fungi within three days.
source: Without any countermeasures the provisions will be completely overgrown by mold fungi within three days (Figure 1B), and the beewolf larva becomes infested by fungi or starves to death (Strohm and Linsenmair, 2001; Herzner et al., 2011a).
evidence: Statement with citations to prior work and reference to figure

claim: Beewolf females reduce molding of larval provisions by coating paralyzed bees with ample amounts of unsaturated hydrocarbons.
source: First, beewolf females reduce molding of the larval provisions by coating the paralyzed bees with ample amounts of unsaturated hydrocarbons (Herzner et al., 2007).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work

claim: Embalming changes the physicochemical properties of the prey's surface causing reduced water condensation on the bees.
source: This embalming changes the physicochemical properties of the preys' surface causing reduced water condensation on the bees (Herzner and Strohm, 2007).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work

claim: Due to water deprivation from embalming, germination and growth of fungi is delayed by two to three days.
source: Due to the deprivation of water, germination and growth of fungi is delayed by two to three days (Herzner et al., 2011b).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work

claim: During overwintering, beewolf larvae are protected by antibiotics on their cocoons produced by symbiotic Streptomyces bacteria.
source: Second, during the long period of overwintering in their cocoons beewolf larvae are protected by antibiotics on their cocoons (Kaltenpoth et al., 2005; Kroiss et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work

claim: Beewolf females apply a secretion containing symbiotic Streptomyces bacteria to the ceiling of the brood cell prior to oviposition.
source: Prior to oviposition, beewolf females apply a secretion containing symbiotic Streptomyces bacteria to the ceiling of the brood cell. The secretion is taken up by the larvae and incorporated into the silk threads of their cocoons.
evidence: Description of behavior

claim: Symbiotic bacteria on beewolf cocoons produce several antibiotics that effectively protect the cocoon and larvae against fungus infestation.
source: There, the bacteria produce several antibiotics that effectively protect the cocoon and, thus, the larvae against fungus infestation (Kroiss et al., 2010; Engl et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work

claim: At least 50% of embalmed bees removed from brood cells showed fungus infestation within six days after oviposition.
source: Despite the considerable effect of prey embalming, when removed from brood cells at least 50% of embalmed bees showed fungus infestation within six days after oviposition (Strohm and Linsenmair, 2001).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work

claim: In natural brood cells, only around 5% of beewolf progeny succumb to mold fungi.
source: Since in natural brood cells only around 5% of the progeny succumb to mold fungi (Strohm and Linsenmair, 2001), we searched for an additional antimicrobial defense mechanism that takes effect during the early stages of beewolf development.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work

claim: The offspring of European beewolves develop in subterranean brood cells provisioned with paralyzed honeybee workers.
source: The offspring of these solitary digger wasps develop in subterranean brood cells provisioned by the female wasps with paralyzed honeybee workers (Apis mellifera, Apidae, Hymenoptera) (Strohm and Linsenmair, 2000) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Statement with citation to prior work and reference to figure

claim: The beewolf egg is laid on one of the bees, the larva hatches after three days, feeds for six to eight days, then spins a cocoon.
source: The beewolf egg is laid on one of the bees, the larva hatches after three days, feeds on the bees for six to eight days, then spins a cocoon and either emerges the same summer or hibernates.
evidence: Description of life cycle

claim: The warm and humid microclimate in beewolf brood cells promotes larval development but also favors fast growing, highly detrimental fungi.
source: The warm and humid microclimate in the brood cell promotes larval development but also favors fast growing, highly detrimental fungi (Engl et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement with citation to prior work
